wiki.welcome.title: Welcome, Explorer
wiki.welcome.body:
Welcome to Blocks Beyond the Stars. You begin stranded with a starter ship and a single goal: survive, build, and explore the galaxy one world at a time.

This Codex is your field reference. Browse the Blocks, Items, Blueprints, Ships, Modules and Planets chapters to learn what everything is and does — and read on through these guides for how the galaxy works, from mining and trading to taming and flight. VEGA, your ship's assistant, will chime in as you explore.
wiki.survival.title: Staying Alive
wiki.survival.body:
Three meters keep you breathing:

  • Oxygen drains in vacuum and above the atmosphere. Refill aboard your ship or anywhere breathable.
  • Hunger falls over time — eat food or load rations into your suit dispenser so it feeds you automatically when low.
  • Health regenerates slowly when fed and oxygenated; the Medbay heal-tank is your respawn point.

Your suit energy powers tools, the jetpack, stealth — and your suit's climate control: in extreme heat, cold or vacuum it drains to keep you alive, and once it is empty you slowly take damage. Suit liners cut that drain sharply.

Food from your base: plant seeds on grass or soil to grow berry plants — and build an algae tank at the workshop: place it at your base and it grows filling algae rations from plain water (melt snow or ice if you have no lake nearby).
wiki.mining-crafting.title: Mining & Crafting
wiki.mining-crafting.body:
Aim at a block and hold {key:Mine}. Harder blocks and ores need a better drill tier — see the Blocks chapter for what each needs and drops.

Smelt the common ores into ingots and plates and craft tools, suit upgrades and ship parts at the workshop. The refinery — the forge block, a workbench craft that needs no blueprint (aboard: the refinery module) — is the high-heat station: it alone smelts the rare Tier-2 metals (titanium, cobalt, tungsten, platinum, uranium, neodymium) and refines diamond, carbide and reactor fuel, and it smelts common ores at a higher yield. The transmuter turns surplus terrain into matter dust and back into ore. Your first titanium: the trade console swaps 5 iron ore for 1 titanium ore, and the forge smelts 2 ore into a titanium plate. New recipes are unlocked as blueprints at your ship's cockpit (Blueprints tab), paid with knowledge, data fragments and materials.
wiki.crafting-stations.title: Stations & menu tabs
wiki.crafting-stations.body:
Most of the menu ({key:UiMenu}) works anywhere — but three tabs are tied to a place. Stand next to the right block and the tab lights up; away from it the tab is dimmed, the hint row above the list names the block you need and where the nearest one is (Show marks it on your compass).

  • Hand recipes (bed, campfire, seeds, rations, …) — anywhere, no station needed.
  • Workbench → Crafting tab: the everyday bench — smelts the common ores, builds tools, parts, suit upgrades and building blocks; also disassembles items. Aboard your ship it is the workshop module.
  • Forge → Crafting (refinery recipes): rare Tier-2 metals, diamond, carbide, reactor fuel, higher-yield smelts. No blueprint needed — build it at a workbench. Aboard: the refinery module.
  • Detoxifier → Crafting (detox recipes, e.g. safe meat). Aboard: the detoxifier module.
  • Matter Forge → Crafting (transmuter recipes: terrain → matter dust → ore). Aboard: the transmuter module.
  • Algae Tank → Crafting (algae rations from water). Campfire → Crafting (campfire cooking).
  • Factory terminal → Crafting (that factory's bulk recipes, only inside a spawned factory).
  • Cockpit → Blueprints tab (research) and Map tab (travel). Aboard your ship, at the cockpit block — or at the helm while flying.
  • Workshop module (aboard) → Ship tab: build further ship modules.
  • Heal Tank / Bed: press {key:Interact} to set your spawn point; standing near a heal tank restores you. Crate: {key:DepositToCrate} to stash, {key:LootContainer} to take. Trade console / vendor: barter recipes and trading.

Look at a placed workbench, forge or similar block and the HUD tells you which tab it powers. The Blocks chapter describes every station block; Mining & Crafting explains the recipes themselves.
wiki.prospecting.title: Prospecting & Ore
wiki.prospecting.body:
Every world wears its riches differently — the Planets chapter lists which ores each world type favours and from which depth. As a rule of thumb:

  • Common metals — iron, copper, aluminium, tin — sit close to the surface almost everywhere, from about 2–8 blocks down.
  • Gold and silver lie a little deeper — silver from about 16 blocks, gold from about 18–30; try rocky, desert and savanna worlds.
  • Rare metals — titanium, cobalt, uranium, platinum, tungsten, neodymium — need a Tier-2 drill and reward digging deep on volcanic, crystal and corrupted worlds: titanium and cobalt from about 8–28 blocks, uranium, platinum, tungsten and neodymium from about 44. Metallic and crystal asteroids carry them nearer the surface.
  • Diamond is the deepest prize of all, 46+ blocks down on the harshest worlds (on asteroids from about 36).
  • Oil lies in tar-shelled pockets 40–120 blocks down, on living worlds only — see Oil and Lubricant.

A terrain scanner makes nearby ore glow through the rock ({key:Place}) and listens for oil pockets up to 800 m away, and a planet scanner on your ship tells you which ores a whole world holds, how common they are and from which depth. The hand scanner finds no ore — it names what a block yields and earns knowledge for every new find.
wiki.oil.title: Oil and Lubricant
wiki.oil.body:
Crude oil lies only under living worlds — worlds with plants and animals — in sealed pockets 40–120 blocks below the normal ground. A pocket is a wide, flat lens of still, black oil inside a shell of tar. Oil never flows, it burns, and you cannot breathe in it. A pocket is finite: what you pump out is gone. The Planets chapter marks the world types that hold oil, and your ship's Deep scanner tells you for a whole world.

Finding it.

  • Tar seeps — on newer worlds about one pocket in three reaches the surface: a black tar patch with a small oil puddle in the middle. Under it a column of soft tar runs straight down to the pocket — dig along the black trail.
  • The oil echo — every pulse of the terrain scanner also listens for oil: the nearest pocket within 800 m shows up as a ping on your compass and your map, and the scanner tells you how far away and how deep it lies.
  • Close up, the scanner makes the oil itself glow violet through the rock.

Harvesting it. Research the titanium drill, then the fluid pump in the Blueprints tab, and build the pump at the workshop. Dig to the tar shell (any tool breaks tar), aim at the oil and use {key:Place}: one cell per pull, a little suit energy each. A drill cannot mine oil — only the pump takes it.

Refining it. The refinery (a ship module; its recipes sit under “Forge” in the crafting menu) turns 1 oil into 3 polymer, or 1 oil and 1 carbon into 2 lubricant. Everything that drills or drives needs lubricant: the jump generator that takes your ship to other star systems, the diamond drill, the mining beam, the auto-drills Mk2 and Mk3, the drill laser, the speeder, the fabricator, the clone tank, the asteroid breaker and the monorail. A dozen oil covers all of it.

No oil in sight? The refinery also makes bio-lubricant: 3 biofuel and 1 carbon give 1 lubricant. Biofuel comes from berries and plant fibre (by hand) or from the algae tank — slower than oil, but it works on every world. Polymer has other routes too: the factory, the workshop and the algae tank.
wiki.knowledge.title: Knowledge & Blueprints
wiki.knowledge.body:
New recipes are unlocked as blueprints (Blueprints tab, at your ship's cockpit), paid for with data fragments and knowledge.

You gather them in many ways: mine glowing data caches in the deep rock, crack open data cubes scattered on the surface (see Data Cubes), scan creatures, plants and blocks you've never seen — a better scanner earns more — and tame wild creatures for a first-time bonus. Crystal worlds are especially rich in caches.

The bio lab pays knowledge too: the first analysis of every species, more for a rare one.
wiki.travel.title: Space Travel
wiki.travel.body:
Launch from a landing pad to enter flight, then open the Map to pick a destination. You can fly and land manually, or quick-travel to a body you have already visited. A hyperjump carries you to another star system entirely.

Each world you land on and each system you enter is remembered — they are recorded on your Map. The Planets chapter explains what to expect from each kind of world.
wiki.frontier.title: The Frontier
wiki.frontier.body:
The further a star system lies from your home system, the more it pays to go there. Frontier systems carry a Frontier tag on the Map — even before you know their name.

Out there, worlds hold richer veins of the rare ores (titanium, cobalt, uranium, platinum, tungsten, neodymium, diamond), bury an extra vault, raise an extra monument, and structure caches hide better salvage. Your starter ores are the same everywhere — the frontier is where you fly once your drill is good enough to want more.

Two world options shape it: Frontier danger (off unless the admin enables it) makes the machines out there tougher — richness and risk together. And a world created with the Growing universe size adds a brand-new system whenever someone hyperjumps into one of the outermost ones: the galaxy grows at your frontier.
wiki.relays.title: SPS Relays
wiki.relays.body:
Before the fall, the Scout and Pioneer Service held the galaxy together with a network of jump relays. Rebuilding it is the great work after the story ends — and you can start any time.

Any commissioned player station can be converted into a relay: open it on the Map and deliver the bill of materials in person — bulk metal plates, circuit boards and reactor fuel from the refinery. Everyone can chip in; the meter is shared, so a crew finishes a relay far faster than one pilot alone.

Two finished relays in neighbouring systems link into a jump lane: along a lane you can hyperjump without a jump generator — your friends' small ships too. Build relays where you travel most, and the network does the jumping for you. Lane routes show a ⇄ mark on the Map.

The network changes the world around it: a relay system draws traders — expect more freighters where a relay hums. And on a world with the Growing universe size, a lane that reaches one of the outermost systems grows the galaxy beyond it: where the network reaches, new stars appear.
wiki.fast-travel.title: Getting Around
wiki.fast-travel.body:
Finding your way: the round compass at the bottom right turns with you — the top of the dial is the way you look, and the N that moves around it marks north. A blue arrow on the rim points the way to your ship and stays readable however far off it is; the blue square inside the dial is the ship itself and the amber pin a waypoint, and the number under each is the distance in metres. Turn until the ship sits at the top and walk. {key:PlanetMap} opens the planet map (north-up, with a legend); click it to set a waypoint. Beacons you plant and markers you save show up on both.

In flight, {key:FlightMap} opens the system chart — a top-down map of the system you are in; click a body to target it. Its Hyperspace tab shows the whole galaxy as stars: the ringed star is where you are, named stars are systems you have visited, a ? is one you have never entered. Click a star and, with a jump generator aboard (or a relay jump lane), hyperjump to it right from the chart.

On foot, you can climb walls and cliffs, a jetpack lifts you over them and a packable speeder covers ground fast, and a boat (workshop: wood, a little iron, no blueprint) carries you across lakes and seas with your head dry. To cross a whole world, fly your ship.

A suit teleporter opens a small destination picker: recall instantly to your ship's heal-tank — handy when you're cornered or overloaded — or, online, beam to an ally standing on the same planet (you arrive right beside them). It needs suit energy and a short cooldown, and won't fire in open space. Plant radio beacons as glowing landmarks so you can always find your way back to a dig site or base.
wiki.climbing.title: Climbing Walls
wiki.climbing.body:
On planets, moons and asteroids you can climb any solid wall — a cliff, a canyon wall, a tree trunk, the side of a house. Jump at the wall, push towards it and hold {key:Jump}: you hold on. Walking along a wall never sticks you to it, and a one-block step is still simply jumped onto. A two-block wall needs no climbing at all: run at it, jump and keep pushing, and you pull yourself over on the way up. Holding {key:Jump} at a wall also catches a fall.

On the wall you hold on as long as you hold {key:Jump}. Push towards the wall to climb up, pull away to climb down, move along it sideways — or just hold {key:Jump} to hang still. Let go of {key:Jump} and you slide down the wall, never fast enough to hurt; press it again to stop. {key:Crouch} drops you off the wall (from high up, that fall hurts). At the top you pull yourself over the edge by yourself; if there is no room up there, or the edge gives no hold, a message tells you so. Mining and building keep working while you hang there.

Your grip tires, and you feel it: you climb slower, then you tremble and breathe hard, and in the end you slide down slowly — never fast enough to hurt. Standing on the ground or on a ladder rung gives your hands a rest. Light worlds are kind to climbers: on an asteroid you get roughly twice as far as on a normal planet, on a heavy world less.

Glass is too smooth to hold, ice only holds with climbing claws, and sand, snow and ash crumble under your hands. Climbing gloves (Suit research, workshop) make your hands tire much more slowly; climbing claws, made from the gloves, last longer still and grip ice, sand and snow like rock. Wear them in a module slot. With a jetpack, holding {key:Jump} keeps you flying; when its energy runs out at a cliff, holding it grabs the wall instead of letting you fall.
wiki.wormholes.title: Wormholes
wiki.wormholes.body:
Very rarely a wormhole opens at the edge of a star system: a glowing, jagged tear in space, dark inside, with the stars of another system shining through. A standard galaxy has exactly one pair of them to find (the world option Wormholes sets how many).

Fly up to the rift and press {key:Interact} (the same as for landing and docking): you come out at its twin in another star system — no jump drive needed. Every wormhole works both ways: fly back through the rift to return.

Where one leads is unknown ("???") until you fly through it or read it with your ship scanner. From then on a violet zigzag on the hyperspace chart shows the pair. Wormholes are found in ordinary systems only — never in the story's special places.
wiki.scanner.title: The Ship Scanner
wiki.scanner.body:
Every ship has a scanner — the cockpit carries it. In flight it sits on the last slot of the bar at the bottom, after the weapons and the tractor beam. Pick it, point the nose at something and hold the fire button until the ring is full: four brackets lock on, a fan of light reaches out from the nose, a hologram sweeps the target — and a card with the result opens on the right. Let go too early and nothing happens: the line under the target says which button to hold.

The scanner reads asteroids (which resources they hold), wrecks (their cargo), anomalies (strange readings that teach you something new — every one of them), life pods (someone is inside — fly close to rescue them), stations, Guardian machines and raiders, and the wormholes (where they lead).

Point it at a planet or moon of the system and you get a planet overview: air, temperature, gravity, weather, water and lava, plants, animals, machines, terrain and buildings — green is harmless, yellow means take care, red is dangerous. The first overview of every world pays a little knowledge.

Upgrades: the Deep scanner (blueprint, built with a sensor lens from the workbench) reaches twice as far, scans faster and shows a planet's ores. The Quantum scanner (built with a quantum sensor) reaches farthest, shows rare ores and hidden data caches — and holding the scan on empty space reads the whole system: for a minute every object out there shows on the radar.
wiki.trading.title: Traders & Markets
wiki.trading.body:
There is no money in the galaxy — everything is barter. Bring goods a trader wants and swap them for what you need. Each trade post is run by a vendor with their own leaning — miners, traders, researchers or settlers — so different stalls offer different wares.

You'll find trade posts in settlements and aboard space stations. Now and then a travelling trader drops out of the sky and parks on a landing pad for 10–15 minutes — busy systems (those with stations) see them most. While one is down, your planet map ({key:PlanetMap}) shows a gold ship marker with the trader's name and your compass a gold blip, so you can walk straight over. It never takes off while you are nearby or trading — only once nobody has been close for a little while.
wiki.settlements.title: Settlements & Towns
wiki.settlements.body:
Breathable worlds — jungle, ocean, savanna, temperate and the like — are dotted with settlements, from lonely hamlets to bustling towns and cities. Each holds settlers, a trade post and a mission board. Their blocks are protected, so you can't mine a town apart.

Talk to people: walk up to anyone and press {key:Interact} (away from a station block). Settlers chat, vendors gossip once they know you, and some conversations offer real choices — what you pick can raise a friendship, hand you something, or make someone call you on the radio later. And keep your eyes open: a few faces return across the galaxy, and they remember you wherever you meet them.

Not every settlement still stands. Ruins are the collapsed remains of fallen ones — unprotected, free to dig through, and often hiding loot. See Ruins & Treasure for what they hold.
wiki.stations.title: Space Stations
wiki.stations.body:
Orbiting some worlds are space stations — havens you can board from space when you fly close. Inside you'll find a hangar to dock, a heal-tank to patch up and respawn, a trade post and a mission board, all in breathable air.

Stations come in every size, from tiny outposts to colossal hubs, and the systems that have them tend to draw the most traders. Want one of your own? Deploy a station core on a spacewalk and build it yourself.
wiki.base-air.title: Bases on Airless Worlds
wiki.base-air.body:
A base core is your life support on a world without air. It breathes air into the 17-block cube around it unconditionally — and into every sealed room connected to it, room by room, as far as 48 blocks from the core.

Three rules decide whether a room seals:

  • Airtight walls, floor and roof — stone, metal, concrete, glass and machines seal. Dirt, sand, mud, snow and other loose ground leak, and so does every shaped (non-cube) block.
  • Only the energy door holds the air in. Hinge, slide and wood doors are open holes to the fill. Rooms chain through energy doors: a sealed room behind a sealed room breathes too.
  • Connected to the core. The chain has to reach the core's cube through energy doors.

Check it: aim at your own core — the prompt shows how many cells and rooms have air and whether the spot you stand on does (here: air). The HUD names your life-support source, and a cyan dome marks the cube on airless worlds. When a wall is mined or a door pulled, the base warns everyone in reach that it is no longer airtight.

The core keeps the wildlife out. Within 24 blocks of the core (height included) no ground or cave animal spawns at all, walls or not. Farther out, a closed ring of walls within 48 blocks of the core does the same job — the ring has to be at least two blocks high and closed all the way round at the level of your feet; a roof is not needed, and any solid block will do (loose ground seals no air, but it stops animals fine). A single gap, an open wooden or hinge door, or a neighbouring area that has not loaded yet lets them in; sliding and energy doors count as walls whatever their state. Fliers ignore both the radius and the walls, cave dwellers come in under the walls, and Guardian machines are not deterred: those are what the sentry post is for. Admins can read the fill for a yard with /basewalls.
wiki.crystal-net.title: The Crystal Net
wiki.crystal-net.body:
Crystal conduits carry one simple signal: ON or OFF. Lay a line of them from a crystal switch to a lamp — everything the line touches is one network, and while the signal is on a glow runs along the wire, away from the switch that sends it. No strengths, no colours, nothing hidden: you can read a circuit by looking at it. Research Crystal Net in the Blueprints tab (after the comm radio); every part is crafted at a workshop from a crystal. Everything works with the usual {key:Interact}: a switch flips and stays, a button gives one short pulse, a device with settings opens a small menu.

Who talks, who listens. Only sources switch a network on: the switch, the button, the step plate, the sensors, the watcher and the signal receiver — plus the logic block, the timer block, the dice block and the Device Eye, which send into the wire their arrow points to. Every other device only listens to its wire; when it has news, a small amber light on top of it turns on.

Six directions. A device with an arrow (logic block, timer block, dice block, watcher, Device Eye, piston, bridge motor) points the way you looked when you placed it — look steeply up or down while placing and it points up or down. Placed wrong? Open its menu and press Turn: it steps through the four sides, up and down.

Yours and your alliance's. Only you and your alliance can use your devices; anyone else just sees "only the owner's alliance". A door you hung follows only your own wires. Pre-built circuits — the light switch in a station's arrival hall, the lamp in a settlement flat, the puzzle niche of a crystal vault — belong to the world: everyone may flip them, only an admin re-wires them.

Aboard your ship. Switches, buttons, plates, proximity sensors, logic, timer and dice blocks, Device Eyes, sounds, lamps, phase blocks, trapdoors, displays, signal senders and receivers and the ship sensor work in your own ship — and the ship's doors follow its wires. The ship's net runs while the ship is parked (landed, or with you inside out in space) and rests in flight. Drills, machines and moving blocks stay decoration aboard. The ship sensor tells the wire whether the hull is damaged or low, the shield is empty, the ship has landed or is docked.

Where and how much. On planets, moons, asteroids, your own stations and your own ship — and only while someone is on that world. A network holds up to 256 blocks; a world 64 networks and 32 sensors, and one player may use half of each, so a crowded server never locks anyone out; 8 sounds can play at once. Beyond a limit a device simply does nothing, and VEGA says so. Machines that were running when you left catch up for a while when you come back (one hour by default; a world option) — VEGA tells you what they did.
wiki.crystal-devices.title: Crystal Net: senses, displays and signals
wiki.crystal-devices.body:
Senses. A step plate is ON while someone stands on it (anyone, players, only your alliance, or animals), a proximity sensor while something is near, a daylight sensor by day or by night, a storage sensor when the crate beside it is full, empty or holds enough of one thing, and a watcher pulses when the block in front of it changes. The environment sensor watches where it stands: no air, too hot, too cold, a storm, toxic air — or, inside your base, an enemy in the base or your alliance at home.

Thinking. A logic block combines signals (AND, OR, NOT, XOR), a timer block shapes them (delay, clock, counter, toggle), and the dice block passes a pulse only now and then — one in 2, 3, 4 or 6 — and sparkles when it does. The Device Eye tells the wire what a machine is doing: a matter sender that cannot send, a full drill, a growing clone tank, a ripe tray or pot, a sentry with a target, someone healing in a heal tank, lying in a bed or sitting on a seat — and, looking into a doorway, whether the door is open.

Showing. A display floats its answer above itself: one symbol for ON and another for OFF (a star, a heart, an arrow, a note …), its own short text while ON, or a counter of how often its wire switched on (reset in its menu). An alarm siren wails while its network is ON, a chime rings once per pulse, a horn carries farther, a melody block plays one note per pulse, and an announcer shows a short line to you and your allies.

Without a wire. A signal sender passes its wire's level to every signal receiver you pair with it — anywhere on the same world. Name your receivers in their menu. The remote control: use it while aiming at a receiver to pair it, use it anywhere else to flip that receiver on or off — the garage door from the garden.

Things that already listen. Lay a conduit beside them and they join: a lamp goes dark when OFF, a door is held open when ON and locked when OFF, a force field opens while ON (a whole field wall switches as one), an energy fence or energy gate lets animals through, a campfire or forge burns only while ON, a heal tank stops healing when OFF, a flower pot or hydro tray harvests into the crate beside it on a pulse, a beam block beams whoever stands on it, a radio beacon turns its marker red, a sentry post holds its fire when OFF, a thumper starts on a pulse and a water spout stops when OFF. Their own use stays as it was: a wired forge is still a forge, a wired bed still a bed.
wiki.crystal-machines.title: Crystal Net: machines and moving blocks
wiki.crystal-machines.body:
Machines. A matter sender beams one stack from a crate beside it into a crate beside its named matter receiver — anywhere on the same world. An auto-drill digs the square below itself (Mk1 5×5, Mk2 7×7, Mk3 9×9) into a crate beside it, only ore or everything, and never touches water, lava or anything a player built; the drill laser cuts straight down. A fabricator crafts one chosen recipe per pulse from the crates around it — and with a station block beside it it can do that station's recipes too: next to a forge it smelts, next to a campfire it cooks. A caller brings peaceful animals and your companions for a while, and a clone tank grows a wild animal you have scanned or tamed on this world (or, with the bio lab, from a sample). Every machine takes from and fills any crate on any of its six sides.

Moving blocks. They never hurt anyone and never close onto anyone — a block that would shut on a player or an animal simply waits.

  • A phase block is a wall block that turns into shimmering air while its network is ON — a secret door. Phase blocks side by side open together, and you can dye them to match your wall.
  • A trapdoor is a hatch in the floor: ON folds it open and you drop through (the fall never hurts), OFF closes it.
  • A bridge motor lays a bridge the way its arrow points while ON — one plank at a time, 2 to 12 long (its menu) — and takes it up again when OFF.
  • A piston pushes up to 4 blocks in front of it one step on ON; set it to sticky and it pulls the first one back on OFF. It never moves crates, devices, doors or someone else's base.
  • A lift: a lift motor at the bottom, a 3×3 platform rides the shaft above it, and a lift stop beside the shaft on each landing. Press a stop (or send it a pulse) and the platform comes to that floor; a pulse on the motor sends it to the next stop. Stand on the platform and it carries you; it waits while anything stands below it.

While you are away. Your base sleeps when nobody is on the world. Machines that were running when the last player left — drills, lasers, senders, fabricators, harvesting pots and trays — catch up for a while when someone comes back (one hour by default, a world option), and VEGA tells you what they did. Timers, sounds and moving blocks only start again with you.
wiki.crystal-recipes.title: Crystal Net: circuits to build
wiki.crystal-recipes.body:
Six circuits to build right away. Purple squares are crystal conduits — a bright one is ON —, the cyan arrow shows where a gate sends.

Night light. A daylight sensor set to night, a line of conduits, a lamp at the end: it switches on by itself after dark.

Doorbell. A step plate outside, the wire under the wall, a chime inside — it rings whenever someone steps on the plate.

Secret door. Two phase blocks in the wall, a hidden switch and a wire to them: flip the switch and the wall opens.

Airlock. One switch touches the inner door; its wire also runs into a logic block set to NOT, which sends into a short wire of its own beside the outer door. Switch ON: the inner door is held open and the outer one locked. Switch OFF: the other way round. Never both at once.

Lift. The lift motor at the bottom of a 3×3 shaft, a landing on each floor with a lift stop beside the shaft. Press a stop to call the platform.

Lucky dice. A button, a dice block, a lamp: press the button and the lamp lights only now and then — set the chance in the dice block's menu.

Stuck? A lamp that stays dark usually means a gap: every piece must touch the next one face to face. A gate that does nothing usually points the wrong way — open its menu and press Turn.
wiki.missions.title: Missions & Jobs
wiki.missions.body:
Mission boards at settlements and stations post an endless run of jobs — mine this, deliver that, travel there. Accept one at the board, complete the objective, and return to the same board to claim your reward in goods.

VEGA hands you a few starter tasks too. Missions are a steady way to earn materials and a sense of direction in the early game.
wiki.factories.title: Factories & Production Terminals
wiki.factories.body:
Some breathable worlds hide a rare factory — an industrial hall whose presses, rotors and conveyors run nonstop, with a factory terminal by the door. No two are built alike.

Stand near the terminal and craft from the Factory category. Factory recipes turn cheaper, less-rare materials into the same goods as the workshop, but in bulk — more input, fewer steps. The catch: each factory only makes the few items on its own roster, so some recipes ask you to find a different factory, and factory crafts can't be taken apart again.

Crafting at a factory is free for anyone. But a factory is read-only until you claim it: stand at the terminal with an SPS access code and press {key:Interact}. That spends the code and makes the factory your base — you and your allies can rebuild it, and the claim sticks across reloads.
wiki.mysteries.title: Mysteries of the Galaxy
wiki.mysteries.body:
Some places exist only once in the whole galaxy. Travellers speak of a shrine that sings, tended by quiet keepers; of a sealed observatory whose dome still watches a sky that went wrong; and of a drifting wreck the charts call The Long Quiet. Where they are, nobody writes down — but a true friend among the settlers or traders will tell you, and mark your map.

Space keeps its own surprises: now and then a life pod drifts through a system — fly close and you save whoever is inside (they will remember you). And sometimes the sensors catch an anomaly no catalogue explains: scan it, and the archive grows a little stranger.

None of it bites. Every mystery is safe to visit on every world setting — bring curiosity, not cannons.
wiki.ruins-and-treasure.title: Ruins & Treasure
wiki.ruins-and-treasure.body:
Ruins are the collapsed remains of fallen settlements — broken walls, a lone half-standing tower, and rubble reclaimed by flora. Unlike bases and stations they are not protected: every block is yours to mine, and what you clear stays cleared. VEGA may warn of structural echoes nearby — bring a scanner and dig around.

Treasure chests are lootable caches hidden away from towns. Each is looted only once and holds richer salvage than ordinary finds — and they are the main world source of a rare SPS access code, the item that lets you claim a factory as your own base. You can also buy a code from a trader's Market, but it's steep. Keep any code you find.
wiki.monuments.title: Monuments & Runes
wiki.monuments.body:
Somebody was here long before you. Monuments are what they left standing: a half-collapsed arcade of arches, a gate that leads nowhere, a ring of standing stones, a weathered obelisk, a rune altar. A world carries up to three, never two of the same kind — and they are the only structure you also find on airless moons, because whoever raised them did not need air either.

Every one of them is carved with glowing runes. Point a scanner at the runes where they stand and you read the inscriptions themselves: far more knowledge than identifying a stone, and a new entry in your Codex. Each kind of monument pays once per planet, so the stone circle on the next world is worth the walk too. A rune you mined and carried home is only a material.

The masonry is freely mineable like a ruin's, and roughly one relic in three hides a small cache nearby.
wiki.creatures.title: Creatures & Wildlife
wiki.creatures.body:
Every world breeds its own creatures, each a one-of-a-kind species shaped by that world. Some graze and wander, some flee at the sight of you, some defend their patch, and a few hunt — only the aggressive ones will come for you, so no world is all teeth. Watch their habits: many sleep through part of the day or night.

Defeated or harvested creatures may drop meat (good food) or a toxic gland (don't eat it). But there's a friendlier path — see Taming.

Begging herds. Some worlds breed peaceful grazers that live in big herds of eight or more — and some of those herds have a nose for food. Hold anything edible (berries, grain, a ration, cooked meat — nothing poisonous) and a herd nearby comes hopping over, circles you and calls; put the food away and they trot off. Press {key:FeedCreature} to throw them one piece: they rush it, squabble over it for a moment, eat it and leave. The scanner tells you which animals do this ("comes running for food").

Bipeds. On newer worlds some animals walk upright on two legs, with two arms and a big head — from knee-high to child-high. They are always peaceful and never alone; many beg with both arms up, chattering something like "meins, meins!". Hurt one and the whole herd runs away. The best known is Mini-Michi-Paul, invented by Paul and Ben of the school club: a knee-high yellow biped that lives in herds of ten on the tropical worlds and loves bananas.
wiki.taming.title: Taming & Companions
wiki.taming.body:
With a creature translator in hand, step up to a wild creature and begin to win its trust. It will signal a mood; answer it the right way — offer the bait it craves, calm it, approach slowly, or give it space — and trust grows. A wrong move can spook a shy creature into bolting, so read it carefully.

Carry the right bait — plant forage, fresh meat or sweet nectar. Tame a creature and it becomes a loyal companion that follows you on its home world. You can keep a handful at once, rename them, and release any you choose. A first tame of a new species also earns you knowledge.

Want your animals to stay put? Craft an energy fence at a workbench and ring in a pen — no creature, wild, tamed or hostile, can cross the humming pylons. Add an energy gate as the entrance: you and settlement folk walk straight through its membrane, while creatures bounce off. Only flying beasts glide over a fence.

Taming by feeding. On newer worlds every begging herd loves one food — the scanner tells you which ("Loves: Banana"). Throw them their favourite food with {key:FeedCreature} twice, and the animal that eats the second piece stays with you as a companion — no translator needed. Mini-Michi-Paul needs two bananas.

Samples. A companion brings a sample of its species along with its gift, and the sampler takes one from any living animal without hurting it — see The Bio Lab for what a sample is good for.
wiki.bio-lab.title: The Bio Lab
wiki.bio-lab.body:
Every plant, every animal and every ore vein carries a substance of its own — and what it does depends on where and how it lives. What survives beside lava tends to protect from heat, what climbs helps you climb, what lives in water helps you breathe. The bio lab finds it out. There are no recipes: what a mix does follows from what goes in, and the same things always give the same result.

Samples. Harvest a plant, fell a tree, mine ore or defeat an animal, and you get one sample on top of the usual yield. Samples collect in your sample case, a compartment of its own in the inventory, so they never fill your backpack. The sampler takes one from a living animal without hurting it (a hostile one has to be held in stasis first — except a giant, which cannot be frozen and is sampled from far away), and a companion brings one along with its gift.

Analyse. Research Bio Lab in the Blueprints tab — it needs no other blueprint first. Build the lab at a workshop and place it on the ground, in your base or on your own station. Aboard your ship the lab is a ship module: build the Bio Lab module in the Ship tab, and the workshop station opens it ({key:Interact} asks: workshop or bio lab) — landed and out in space. A lab block built into a ship is only decoration. One lab is enough for everything. Stand next to it and press {key:Interact}. Analysing uses up one sample and shows what the species carries: its effect, its strength from I to XV, its rarity, how long it lasts and whether it has a catch. The first analysis of a species pays knowledge. Until then your scanner only says that the substance is unknown.

Mix. One sample alone gives a plain extract. With Synthesis you add three more things. A carrier decides the form: water makes an injector (strong and short), plant fibre a gel (weak and very long), berries, grain or fruit a bar (it also feeds you), salt a capsule, oil a coating for tools. A stabiliser — a mineral sample or an ingot — steadies the mix, and the right one takes the catch away. A second sample reacts with the first: it amplifies it, weakens it, adds its own effect, or turns the effect into a related one. Which groups do what to each other is the same on every world. A shaky mix can fail and its ingredients are lost — but your handbook remembers every mix you have tried and shows its result beforehand the next time. A detoxifier next to you and one carbon wash toxic samples as part of the mix — the lab says beforehand whether it will, and a washed mix is its own entry in your handbook.

Effects. Take a preparation like food. Up to three effects run at once: Speed, Jump, Feather Fall, Grip, Shield, Regeneration, Strength, Mining, Reflex, Breath, Heat Ward, Cold Ward, Toxin Ward, Satiety, Night Sight, Perception, Stealth, Energy and Gathering. A catch is always mild — more hunger, a little slower, a lower jump — never damage. Some substances run out faster in great heat or great cold — aboard your ship or a station the air is always comfortable.

Rarity is found. Common worlds and easy animals give weak substances. The strong ones live where it is hard to get: rare worlds, caves, lava, dangerous animals — and the giants.

Materials. A material is the same everywhere — copper conducts on every world — but every world's deposit has its own purity and small quirks, and those count in the lab. With the Lab Tuning blueprint, the lab's Change tab improves a drill, a weapon or a piece of suit gear with a material — a coating adds a second gain but is optional (see Improving Items): hard hits harder, conductive saves energy, light makes a tool faster, magnetic adds reach or grip. A big change has a price — a bit slower, a bit heavier. The tier of a tool never changes, and you can wash a change off again. The piece has to lie in your backpack — take suit gear off first.

Cloning and crossing. The clone tank also grows animals from the samples in your case — on any world, as long as a water animal finds water and a lava animal lava. With Crossing you give the tank a partner: two species become a new one, with the body of one parent and the colours of the other. The same parents always give the same child, a cross is never hostile, and you get a sample of the new species to clone it or cross it again. If your sample case has no room for it, the tank waits with its light on until you make room. Two plant samples give a new plant with a new form. The lab raises a seedling from any plant sample: plant it on clean ground, on a hydro tray or in a flower pot — on any world whose air is neither toxic nor corrosive, in your base or on a station.
wiki.item-tuning.title: Improving Items
wiki.item-tuning.body:
Your drill, a weapon or a piece of your suit can be improved in the bio lab. In the lab the tab is called Change, and the blueprint that unlocks it is Lab Tuning — all three words mean the same thing.

The way there. Research Bio Lab at the cockpit (no other blueprint needed), build the lab at a workshop and set it up on the ground, in your base or on a station — or build the bio lab ship module and open the lab at your ship's workshop station. Then research Lab Tuning: the lab's third tab, Change, opens.

What goes in. Tool or gear: a drill, a weapon or a suit piece that protects. It has to lie in your backpack or hotbar — worn gear does not show up, take it off first. Material (needed): a mineral sample from your sample case, or a material from your backpack such as an ingot, an ore or a crystal. Coating (optional): a preparation you mix in the Mix tab with oil or lubricant as the carrier (that needs Synthesis). It adds a second gain when its effect fits.

Which material does what. On a drill or weapon: hard, heavy or unstable materials (iron, lead, tungsten, uranium) hit harder; conductive ones (copper, gold) save energy; heat-proof or light ones shorten the cooldown; magnetic ones add range. A tool only gains what it has — a basic drill uses no energy and has no range, so only hitting harder works on it. On suit gear: hard or heavy means more armour, heat- or cold-proof more insulation, light better fall protection, magnetic more grip, conductive more oxygen. The lab shows the result before you press the button, and lists the materials you carry that work on the piece.

The price. A small change is free. A big one (three levels or more) has a small price — a tool gets a little slower or uses more energy, gear gets a little heavier unless the material is light. The tier of a tool never changes. Wash off takes a change away again, at no cost.
wiki.hazards.title: Air, Weather & Hazards
wiki.hazards.body:
Not every world is kind to lungs. Breathable worlds let you roam freely; toxic worlds drain your suit oxygen — fit an oxygen extractor to pull breathable air from the haze and slow the loss. Airless worlds and open space give nothing back, so watch your tank.

Temperature is a real hazard in Survival. Roughly −5 to 40 °C is free; beyond that your suit's climate control drains suit energy — the further past the band (an ice world's night, a lava plain at noon, vacuum), the faster. When the energy runs out you slowly take damage, so head back before the bar empties. Your defenses: dig in (a few blocks below the surface every world settles near a mild ground temperature — unless lava or ice sits right next to you), build a roof (shelter halves the stress), wait out the hottest or coldest hours, keep to the ship, and craft suit liners at the workshop — the better the liner, the less the suit spends. Watch the HUD temperature readout: blue is freezing, red is overheating. The world option Environmental hazards turns all of this down or off.

Weather comes in episodes: it builds, holds and fades, and every world has its own temper. Besides rain and storms there is drizzle, fog, gales, blizzards and heatwaves — and the genuinely alien: acid rain on toxic worlds, ember fall on volcanic ones, spore blooms in jungles and swamps, and ion storms and meteor showers that even airless moons get. Fronts drift across the world, so you can watch a storm arrive. Weather can hurt — corrosive and falling weather drains your suit out in the open, and a roof really is the answer — but it can also pay: an ion storm charges an exposed suit, a spore bloom fattens the harvest. Craft the weather scanner to read what is coming. Gravity varies too: on light worlds you'll leap far, on heavy ones every jump costs more. Refill oxygen and energy aboard your ship or at any heal-tank.

Toxic worlds are rare, dead and rich. Nothing grows or lives on their ash and sulphur, and the air is never breathable — but every toxic world rolls its own dangers: on some the air is corrosive and slowly eats your health outdoors (the ship, a station, a base or a sealed room keep it out; a suit liner slows it — the better the liner, the more), on most the water is poison and looks it. In return, rare ores lie just below the surface, sometimes right on top of it, and deep in the caves a little life may hide. VEGA reads each toxic world's air and water for you when you land.

Toxica-Maxima is the poisoned planet itself — at most one in a galaxy. Its air always corrodes, its water always burns, and a green acid thunderstorm never ends; a roof or a factory hall keeps the rain off (every factory hall, on every world, still breathes). Its ground, stone, wood and ore are tainted: diamond, titanium, iron and copper lie right under the surface, but every piece has to be washed at the Decontaminator (2 tainted + 1 carbon → 2 clean) or at one of the planet's abandoned factories. Its animals are contaminated — green-eyed hunters that never sleep — and drop contaminated meat that washes clean the same way.
wiki.colours.title: Colour & Light
wiki.colours.body:
Almost any building material can wear your colour: select the stack in your hotbar, open the slot actions ({key:HotbarAction}) and pick Colour. Dye is free and recolours the whole stack; Glow makes the blocks shine in the chosen colour and costs one crystal per block.

Glass takes dye too — it stays frosted, just coloured. Perfect for stained-glass windows and coloured domes. Want to actually see out? Research Clear Glass (two glass + one polymer at the workshop): a look-through pane for canopies and observation domes that dyes just the same.

The light fixtures — lamps, strip lights, torches, lanterns — accept dye as well, and a dyed lamp casts light in its dye colour, no crystal needed: it already is a light. A dyed torch burns with a coloured flame. Line a corridor with strip lights in your crew's colour. A dyed lantern shows its colour too — a pretty door marker — but its small flame is too faint to light the area; hang a dyed lamp there when you want coloured light.

Doors keep their own look — they are moving fittings, not blocks — and machines, ores and flora stay as they are.
wiki.own-forms.title: Your Own Forms
wiki.own-forms.body:
Blocks come in ready-made forms — slabs, ramps, stairs, pillars — but you can also design your own. Craft the shaping tool at the workshop, use it with {key:Place}, and you get a grid to fill in: one layer at a time, from the floor of the block up to its ceiling, with the layer below showing through dimly so you can stack a shape without losing your place. A little preview turns beside the canvas so you can see what you are building. Give it a name and it is yours.

A saved form lives in My forms in the crafting menu's Forms tab, and you can build it out of any material — the same arch in wood, in stone, in metal. It behaves like every other form after that: place it, turn it, mine it back.

Sharing: point the shaping tool at a block somebody else shaped and their form opens in your editor, ready to save (with their name on it). You can also stamp a form onto a stencil and give that away, or copy a form as a code to send to a friend.

Two things to know: a form can only be so fine — the editor shows how much detail is left — and forms are decoration, so you cannot sit on a chair you designed yourself.
wiki.farming.title: Farming & Foraging
wiki.farming.body:
Flora is everywhere, and most of it gives plant fiber when cut, with some plants offering berries to eat. Watch for toxic berries and glands — they'll hurt rather than heal.

You can grow your own: plant a plant seed or crystal seed on open ground and it will sprout. Many wild plants regrow on their own over time if you leave their roots, so a good foraging spot keeps giving. Load rations into your suit dispenser and it feeds you automatically when hunger bites.

Settlement greenhouses grow three crops — berries, grain and mushrooms — and every one comes with a hand-made seed. With the Field Kitchen blueprint a campfire cooks real meals from them (hearty stew, algae soup, mushroom skewers), and Bio-Refining puts the algae tank and the detoxifier to work: fuel and fibre from algae, toxic berries washed safe, mushroom parts turned into bait.

Fruit trees. On newer worlds about a third of the trees hang fruit under their crowns — round fruit, long fruit, grape clusters or bananas. Every kind of tree on a world bears its own shape in its own colour, so this world's palms may carry orange bananas while its broadleafs hang blue apples. Pick a fruit by hand; it grows back on its leaf after a couple of minutes. A fruit is toxic exactly when its tree is — scan the trunk or the fruit, they answer the same — and the detoxifier washes toxic fruit safe. Fruit is the most filling plant food there is, and begging herds come for it too.

On the newest worlds you may find a grove of Fifi plants — Sophie's plant from the school club: as tall as a tree, with a green trunk, yellow leaves and pink blossoms that glow and light up the night. Berries hang under the leaves; they are always edible and grow back two minutes after you pick them.

Bred plants. The bio lab raises a seedling from any plant sample, and two plant samples in a clone tank give a new plant with a new form. A seedling grows on clean ground, on a hydro tray or in a flower pot, on any world whose air is neither toxic nor corrosive — and it grows back after you harvest it.
wiki.combat.title: Combat & Defence
wiki.combat.body:
When trouble finds you, gear up. Melee tools — from a humble machete to a plasma sword — hit hard up close, while pistols and blasters strike from range; higher tiers cost suit energy but deal far more. Wearing a helmet, chest and leg armour stacks up your damage resistance.

Glove weapons sit on both hands. The shock gloves barely hurt — they push a creature, robot or bandit a few blocks away and leave it dizzy for a second, so it can neither move nor bite. The energy gloves punch fast and hard, left and right. Both draw a little suit energy per hit. Big animals fly less far, giants are far too big to push, and players and pets are never pushed. A push stops at walls and never throws anything off a cliff or into lava.

A stasis projector freezes a charging creature in its tracks, and a stealth suit lets you slip past unseen while it drains energy. In space, expect hostile drones and craft — fit your ship with weapons and shields before you go looking for a fight.
wiki.ships-modules.title: Your Ship & Modules
wiki.ships-modules.body:
Your ship is your home, workshop and ride between worlds. It's built from modules — a cockpit, reactor and life support keep it flying, while a workshop, medbay, cargo holds and more add comforts and capacity.

Unlock and craft bigger hulls in the Blueprints tab — a nimble scout, a roomy hauler, a balanced corvette — and fit them with refineries, a jump generator for crossing star systems, tractor beams, shields and weapons. See the Ships chapter for each hull.
wiki.alliances.title: Allies & Playing Together
wiki.alliances.body:
Online, you can form an alliance with another player — both must agree. Allies share full access to each other's planet bases and space stations: you can build and rebuild together, and you can't harm one another, even on rougher servers.

Allies can also find each other fast: a suit teleporter beams you to any ally standing on the same planet, landing right beside them. Ships always stay personal — an alliance never opens your ship to others (the teleporter refuses while your ally is aboard theirs). Either side can end an alliance at any time. Be kind out there; see the House Rules.

One world can even mix game modes: the world admin can give a single player their own mode — /mode Player creative (or the Player-modes rows on the Character tab) lets a kid fly and build freely while everyone else keeps playing survival. /mode Player world switches them back.
wiki.arcade.title: Data Cubes & Fragments
wiki.arcade.body:
Scattered across some worlds are glowing data cubes — derelict storage terminals. Walk up to one and press {key:Interact} to extract its data fragment into your collection.

Not every world holds one, and a cube's fragment stays a surprise until you reach it. A recovered fragment is yours for good — open the DataQubes tab any time to run it. Your records are kept locally, just for you.
wiki.house-rules.title: House Rules
wiki.house-rules.body:
Blocks Beyond the Stars is a family game — made so that kids can play safely. There is nothing here that isn't suitable for children.

When you play online with others, please keep it friendly:

  • Be kind in radio chat — others may be younger than you.
  • No rude words in chat, or in the names you give players, bases, stations, beacons or creatures.
  • You can mute anyone you don't want to hear, and voice chat can be switched off completely.

What the game itself promises: mild sci-fi scuffles only — no blood, bandits are chased away, never killed, and new worlds start with weapons set to tools only. There is nothing to buy, no ads, and the game never asks for your real name or e-mail.

Server hosts may remove anything inappropriate and block players who break these rules. If someone misbehaves, type /report — a person will look at it.
